lines.text: Our hands are remarkably versatile tools, and English has developed precise vocabulary for every action they perform. Grasping actions range from gentle to forceful: you grip a railing tightly for safety, clutch a bag close in a crowd, clasp someone's hand in greeting, and clench your fist in anger. Finger actions include pinch (squeeze between thumb and finger), poke (push with a finger), flick (sharp, quick finger movement), and tap (light repeated touches). Creative hand actions encompass knead (press and fold dough), mould (shape with hands), carve (cut into shape), and sketch (draw quickly). Cleaning involves scrub (rub hard to clean), wipe (clean by rubbing with a cloth), rinse (wash briefly with water), and polish (rub to make shiny). Destructive actions include smash (break violently), crush (press until broken), tear (pull apart), and shatter (break into many pieces). Delicate actions use words like caress (touch gently and lovingly), stroke (move hand smoothly over something), and fondle (touch tenderly). Communication through hands gives us wave (greeting from a distance), beckon (signal someone to approach), point (indicate direction), and gesture (move hands while speaking). Each verb captures not just the physical motion but the force, intention, and emotion behind it.

lines.text: In British and American culture, a firm handshake is expected in professional settings. A limp handshake ('dead fish') is considered weak; an overly strong one is aggressive. The ideal is firm, brief (2-3 seconds), with eye contact.
